newsitem.title: USA: Teamsters chief cites progress in UPS strike talks.
newsitem.headline: Teamsters chief cites progress in UPS strike talks.

text.p: Teamsters union President Ron Carey said on Sunday that marathon talks with United Parcel Service had made strides toward ending the two-week-old strike by 185,000 workers against the giant package delivery firm.

Carey's assessment was the first indication from either side that the talks were progressing since negotiators moved into a Washington hotel at the request of Labor Secretary Alexis Herman on Thursday morning.

"There has been some movement," Carey said in explaining why he believed he was right not to put the company's previous so-called "last and final" offer to his members for a vote as UPS executives had been urging.

"We are talking about the issues and that to me is progress -- trying to see if we can find some areas of agreement and the talks are moving along," Carey said on the NBC television program, "Meet the Press."
Company and union negotiators continued meeting on Sunday at a hotel across the street from the International Brotherhood of Teamsters headquarters.
Asked if the union planned to stay at the bargaining table until a deal was reached, Carey said, "Absolutely."

UPS Chairman James Kelly, appearing on the same program, also sounded an optimistic, though cautious, note, saying that negotiators were discussing "dozens and dozens of issues" but it was unclear when an agreement could be reached.
"The fact that we're continuing to talk is encouraging," Kelly said, reiterating that the company would use replacement workers only as a last resort.
The two sides have been meeting in face-to-face sessions, with federal mediators and with Herman since Thursday morning, taking only a few brief sleep breaks along the way.

Herman, who also has encamped herself at the hotel and was credited by both sides with helping to keep the talks moving, is scheduled to fly to Los Angeles on Monday morning for a speaking engagement.

The walkout by drivers, loaders and sorters on Aug. 4 has crippled the nation's largest package delivery firm to the tune of an estimated $300 million a week in lost revenues and has cost UPS more than a half-billion dollars so far.
Kelly said the strike could take a lasting bite out of the company's 80 percent market share, which would translate into fewer jobs when the dispute was settled.
"Our customers have been devastated in many cases," he said. "Unfortunately a lot of that business has gone away ... and a lot of that business isn't coming back."
UPS competitors, including the U.S. Postal Service, have rushed to try to fill the void. But many small businesses are feeling the pinch of being unable have their goods delivered.

An Oklahoma lawyer announced on Saturday that he filed a federal lawsuit against UPS on behalf of a number of small and medium-sized companies, charging the shipper with breach of contract and negligence and seeking at least $75,000, the minimum required in federal court.
Buoyed by opinion polls showing the strikers winning the public relations battle, Carey has stuck to his theme that UPS convert more part-time jobs into higher paying full-time jobs.
CNN reported Saturday that a Gallup poll showed 55 percent of Americans backing the strikers.
For its part, UPS has been seeking the withdrawal of its pension plan from its current multi-employer plan so it can set up a plan solely for Teamster members at UPS.
